lines.t: Okay, let's check. Number one. Diego?
“We had to put off the meeting until Friday.”
Exactly right. “Put off.” You'll also hear “push back”: “We had to push the meeting back.” Same thing.

questions.q: Diego's answer is right. What does Kate say? What does she add?
questions.a: “Exactly right.” Then another way to say it: “You'll also hear ‘push back’.”

lines.t: Number two. Aiko?
“Could you look after my report before I send it?”
Ooh, close! You've got the verb, just not the little word. Look…?
Look… over?
That's it! “Could you look over my report?”

questions.q: Aiko's answer is nearly right. What does Kate praise first?
questions.a: The verb: “You've got the verb, just not the little word.”

questions.q: Does Kate give Aiko the answer?
questions.a: No: “Look…?” Aiko finds “over” herself.

lines.t: Number three. Marco?
“I'm making a photo of the board.”
Mm, not quite. In Italian it's “fare”, isn't it? In English it's “take”: “I'm taking a photo.”
I've been saying “make a photo” for ten years.
Don't worry, you're in good company. Half my students say it.

questions.q: Why does Kate mention Italian?
questions.a: She names the reason for the mistake: in Italian it's “fare”. The mistake makes sense.

questions.q: Marco feels a bit silly. What does Kate say?
questions.a: “Don't worry, you're in good company.” Lots of people say it.

lines.t: But why “take”?
Good question! Honestly, there's no real logic. It's just what goes together. We're doing make, do and take next week.

questions.q: Can Kate explain why it's take? What does she say?
questions.a: Not really, and she's honest about it: “Good question! Honestly, there's no real logic.”

lines.t: Number four. Ewa?
“Sorry, something came out, so I can't make it.”
Nearly! Like Aiko: you've got the verb, just not the little word. Something came…?
Up! Something came up.
Spot on. And it's a great one: you don't have to say what came up.

questions.q: What does Kate say before Something came…?
questions.a: “Nearly!” and, as with Aiko, she credits the verb. Then Ewa finishes it herself.

questions.q: Ewa gets it. What does Kate say?
questions.a: “Spot on.” And she adds why it's a useful phrase.

lines.t: Sorry, quick question about emails…
Hold that thought, Diego. Let's just finish number five. Selin?
“We need to take a decision by Monday.”
“Take a decision” is fine, you'll hear it, especially in British English. It's just that “make a decision” is what most people say.
So both are correct?
Yep, both work. Okay, Diego, your question.

questions.q: Diego interrupts. What does Kate say? Does she forget his question?
questions.a: “Hold that thought, Diego.” No: “Okay, Diego, your question.”

questions.q: Is take a decision wrong? How does Kate put it?
questions.a: No: “It's fine… It's just that ‘make a decision’ is what most people say.”

lines.t: I wrote “I did a mistake” in an email today. Is that okay?
Ah, tricky one. “Fazer” is both “make” and “do” in Portuguese, isn't it? With mistakes, it's “make”: “I made a mistake.”
Oh no. I think I've written that in a lot of emails.
Then you're in very good company. It's one of the most common ones. Last one, Aiko?

questions.q: How does Kate make Diego feel better about his emails?
questions.a: The reason (Portuguese “fazer”) and “Then you're in very good company.”

lines.t: “Can you get back to me about the invoice tomorrow?”
Spot on. “Get back to me” works for anything: email, phone, whatever. “Can you let me know about the invoice tomorrow?” also works.

questions.q: Aiko's last answer is right. What two things does Kate do?
questions.a: She confirms (“Spot on.”) and adds another way: “‘Can you let me know…?’ also works.”

little_words_rule: too at the end: the usual choice in conversation — I've got a one-year-old too.
also before the main verb, but after be and after the first auxiliary or modal — I also wanted to talk about… · It's also pretty lonely. · I've also seen it. · I'll also post it.
a negative → either at the end — It wasn't on my radar either.
В разговоре also встречается примерно раз на 4 500 слов; «тоже» чаще всего — too в конце фразы (в британском разговоре ещё и as well).

body: Я буду группой на обсуждении: кто-то забегает вперёд, кто-то кивает и молчит, кто-то спрашивает то, чего ты точно не знаешь, кто-то говорит длинно и путано.

body: Главное задание урока, два раунда. Раунд 1: коробка открыта. Я — твой класс: проверка упражнения, потом короткое обсуждение.
Раунд 2: новые студенты, новые ответы — коробку закрой и говори по памяти.
Между раундами — мой фидбэк. Потом возвращаешься сюда: then & now.
